title: Who Pays for Thinking? Billing Hidden Reasoning Tokens in Model–Cloud Contracts

paper.title: Who Pays for Thinking? Billing Hidden Reasoning Tokens in Model–Cloud Contracts
paper.abstract: Abstract. In token-priced language model services, users can see the prompts they submit and the answers they receive, but may also pay for internal reasoning and candidate answers that are not shown in the final response. This paper develops a three-party service model to study how charging for this intermediate computation shapes providers’ decisions and social welfare. Users purchase answers from a model firm that pays an execution cloud, with either supplier controlling the computation budget. The model separates user billing from upstream payments and identifies when metered pricing encourages excessive generation, when fixed service prices restrict valuable computation, and how responsibility for execution costs changes these choices. A LiveCodeBench study measures answer quality, latency, token use, and resource consumption across five model deployments, with numerical billing comparisons for the three covered by archived tariffs. At equal average charges on the reference workload, the calibrated comparisons show that billing structure changes both service participation and the computation budgets suppliers select. For accepted services with different budgets, the measured outcomes define the user-value thresholds at which their welfare ranking reverses. Metered pricing yields higher welfare when the additional inference it induces creates net social value, whereas fixed service pricing is preferable when the costs of that computation outweigh its benefits.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications built on large language models (LLMs), including chatbots and coding assistants, have become an important part of the Web. Similarweb estimates that generative AI platforms received an average of 9.5 billion Web visits per month between June 2025 and May 2026 ( Similarweb, 2026 ) . Token-priced AI services can charge for internal reasoning and for candidates that an application generates but does not deliver to its end user ( Google, 2026a ; Google, 2026b ) . How does charging for this unseen generation shape providers’ computation choices, and when does the additional computation create enough value for users to justify its cost? In cloud-hosted services, users pay a model firm that purchases computation from a cloud provider. Existing studies analyze incentives to expand inference, price menus for users with different valuations, and manipulation of reported token counts ( Artola Velasco et al., 2026a ; Bergemann et al., 2026 ; Artola Velasco et al., 2026b ) . These studies focus on the user–provider transaction, leaving the model–cloud allocation of incentives largely implicit. A larger bill can reward the model firm while additional execution costs fall on the cloud, making both the payment between them and control over generation relevant to service provision. This paper compares metered billing for intermediate generation with fixed service pricing at equal average charges on the reference workload. A three-party model separates this retail choice from the payment to the execution cloud and the right to choose the attempt budget. Payments for compute time, fixed capacity fees, and revenue sharing give the suppliers different returns to another candidate. The analysis determines which services satisfy participation and selects the controller’s most profitable budget, retaining ties and exit. It identifies when metered pricing supports more computation and when that computation improves welfare. Pooling, which submits multiple tasks in one generation call, enters through two channels. A lower cost increment can change the cloud’s preferred budget, and lower cost levels can make a previously rejected budget tradable. Either response can lower welfare even when each fixed service becomes cheaper. A study on 106 LiveCodeBench tasks ( Jain et al., 2025 ) measures correct and incorrect delivery, latency, token generation, and resource use across five model deployments. These measurements, together with archived tariffs for three deployments, provide the inputs for the numerical pricing comparison. For these three deployments, metered bills grow faster than execution costs in every measured configuration as the budget increases. At equal average charges on the reference workload, the calibrated comparisons show how these incentives and supplier participation produce different budgets. The welfare analysis identifies when the additional inference induced by metered billing creates enough value to justify its costs and when a fixed service price produces a better outcome. These boundaries depend on the model’s quality gains, execution costs, and the losses users associate with errors and waiting. Supplier profits explain the budget changes, and user purchase thresholds identify where those predicted services can be traded. The contribution is a calibrated comparison of retail pricing under joint and separate supplier participation. Separating the model firm and cloud can leave a jointly profitable service unprovided when the upstream payment assigns a loss to one party. With a fixed capacity fee, the low-budget bill can be too small for the model firm while high-budget cost is too large for the cloud. The integrated benchmark exposes this difference, while measured service profiles determine the available budgets and the user-value conditions governing their welfare.

sections.heading: 4. Experiments
sections.text: The evaluation combines measured service profiles with the contract model to compare metered billing and fixed pricing at equal average charges on the reference workload. It determines participation and budget choice, then identifies the user-value thresholds that reverse their welfare ranking. Sensitivity covers deployments, execution configurations, upstream terms, and resource costs.

sections.heading: 4.1. Experimental setup and calibration
sections.text: The study uses 106 evaluation tasks from LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , with 16 separate tasks reserved for calibration. Five deployments cover Qwen3.8 with thinking enabled and disabled, Qwen3.5 thinking, Nemotron thinking, and Coder. sections.heading: 5.1. Metered pricing and strategic inference
sections.text: Payments for services that users cannot easily evaluate create incentives to change provision or billing, a central concern of credence-goods theory ( Dulleck and Kerschbamer, 2006 ) . Test-Time Compute Games studies strategic inference budgets among competing providers and proposes a price-and-quality auction ( Artola Velasco et al., 2026a ) . Menu pricing derives token-budget contracts for heterogeneous users and extends them to model competition ( Bergemann et al., 2026 ) . Tokenization research studies profitable misreporting and mechanisms for truthful billing ( Artola Velasco et al., 2026b ) . These studies connect user payments to provider behavior. Table 4 locates the present comparison, which holds tariffs and token counts fixed while separating the model firm’s and cloud’s participation decisions.

sections.heading: 5.2. Payments and cost responsibility
sections.text: The allocation of marginal returns and costs is a standard concern of industrial organization ( Tirole, 1988 ) . Revenue-sharing contracts can coordinate retail quantities and prices under specified supply-chain conditions ( Cachon and Lariviere, 2005 ) . Collaborative-service models relate contract choice to the buyer’s and vendor’s contributions to output ( Roels et al., 2010 ) . Cloud services add metered infrastructure and different commitment and availability terms ( Armbrust et al., 2009 ; Amazon Web Services, 2026a ; Amazon Web Services, 2026b ) . Here a fixed user price removes the retail revenue increment, while a fixed capacity fee removes the model firm’s additional upstream payment. The integrated comparison shows how separate cost responsibility can prevent a jointly profitable inference service from being supplied.

sections.heading: 5.3. Quality, selection, and service cost
sections.text: Test-time scaling studies how additional computation improves answer quality ( Snell et al., 2025 ) . Verification and self-consistency determine which gains reach users ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , while imperfect verifiers can limit resampling benefits ( Stroebl et al., 2026 ) . Quality-based and adaptive contracts use automated evaluations to determine payments ( Saig et al., 2024 ; Saig et al., 2026 ) . Serving research changes execution costs through scheduling, key-value (KV) cache management ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Kwon et al., 2023 ) , and the separation or interleaving of prompt processing and token generation ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Agrawal et al., 2024 ) . Analytical inference models link hardware use to efficiency ( Pope et al., 2023 ) . This study measures delivered correctness, errors, latency, and resources through online answer selection, then combines these service profiles with supplier participation to compare billing rules and welfare thresholds.

sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
sections.text: Metered billing rewards additional intermediate computation with additional revenue, while fixed service pricing removes that revenue increment. How this changes the attempt budget depends on control and cost responsibility. Under revenue sharing, metered billing rewards both suppliers for a larger bill. With fixed pricing, the cloud receives the same payment as execution cost rises, while a model firm bearing no additional cost can remain indifferent between budgets. Under a fixed capacity fee, separate participation can block a jointly profitable service that an integrated supplier would provide. Under revenue sharing and user purchase, the calibrated comparisons show that equal average charges on the reference workload can support different computation budgets. Where metered billing induces a larger budget and both resulting services are purchased, it yields higher welfare when the value of additional correct answers exceeds the added error losses, waiting costs, and resource costs. Fixed service pricing yields higher welfare when that balance is reversed. Payments redistribute surplus. Welfare depends on how revenue, cost, and control align private computation choices with net social value.

In token-priced language model services, users can see the prompts they submit and the answers they receive, but may also pay for internal reasoning and candidate answers that are not shown in the final response. This paper develops a three-party service model to study how charging for this intermediate computation shapes providers’ decisions and social welfare. Users purchase answers from a model firm that pays an execution cloud, with either supplier controlling the computation budget. The model separates user billing from upstream payments and identifies when metered pricing encourages excessive generation, when fixed service prices restrict valuable computation, and how responsibility for execution costs changes these choices. A LiveCodeBench study measures answer quality, latency, token use, and resource consumption across five model deployments, with numerical billing comparisons for the three covered by archived tariffs. At equal average charges on the reference workload, the calibrated comparisons show that billing structure changes both service participation and the computation budgets suppliers select. For accepted services with different budgets, the measured outcomes define the user-value thresholds at which their welfare ranking reverses. Metered pricing yields higher welfare when the additional inference it induces creates net social value, whereas fixed service pricing is preferable when the costs of that computation outweigh its benefits. Keywords: reasoning tokens, metered pricing, fixed service pricing, revenue sharing, inference economics, cloud contracts 1. Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) applications built on large language models (LLMs), including chatbots and coding assistants, have become an important part of the Web. Similarweb estimates that generative AI platforms received an average of 9.5 billion Web visits per month between June 2025 and May 2026 ( Similarweb, 2026 ) . Token-priced AI services can charge for internal reasoning and for candidates that an application generates but does not deliver to its end user ( Google, 2026a ; Google, 2026b ) . How does charging for this unseen generation shape providers’ computation choices, and when does the additional computation create enough value for users to justify its cost? In cloud-hosted services, users pay a model firm that purchases computation from a cloud provider. Existing studies analyze incentives to expand inference, price menus for users with different valuations, and manipulation of reported token counts ( Artola Velasco et al., 2026a ; Bergemann et al., 2026 ; Artola Velasco et al., 2026b ) . These studies focus on the user–provider transaction, leaving the model–cloud allocation of incentives largely implicit. A larger bill can reward the model firm while additional execution costs fall on the cloud, making both the payment between them and control over generation relevant to service provision. This paper compares metered billing for intermediate generation with fixed service pricing at equal average charges on the reference workload. A three-party model separates this retail choice from the payment to the execution cloud and the right to choose the attempt budget. Payments for compute time, fixed capacity fees, and revenue sharing give the suppliers different returns to another candidate. The analysis determines which services satisfy participation and selects the controller’s most profitable budget, retaining ties and exit. It identifies when metered pricing supports more computation and when that computation improves welfare. Pooling, which submits multiple tasks in one generation call, enters through two channels. A lower cost increment can change the cloud’s preferred budget, and lower cost levels can make a previously rejected budget tradable. Either response can lower welfare even when each fixed service becomes cheaper. A study on 106 LiveCodeBench tasks ( Jain et al., 2025 ) measures correct and incorrect delivery, latency, token generation, and resource use across five model deployments. These measurements, together with archived tariffs for three deployments, provide the inputs for the numerical pricing comparison. For these three deployments, metered bills grow faster than execution costs in every measured configuration as the budget increases. At equal average charges on the reference workload, the calibrated comparisons show how these incentives and supplier participation produce different budgets. The welfare analysis identifies when the additional inference induced by metered billing creates enough value to justify its costs and when a fixed service price produces a better outcome. These boundaries depend on the model’s quality gains, execution costs, and the losses users associate with errors and waiting. Supplier profits explain the budget changes, and user purchase thresholds identify where those predicted services can be traded. The contribution is a calibrated comparison of retail pricing under joint and separate supplier participation. Separating the model firm and cloud can leave a jointly profitable service unprovided when the upstream payment assigns a loss to one party. With a fixed capacity fee, the low-budget bill can be too small for the model firm while high-budget cost is too large for the cloud. The integrated benchmark exposes this difference, while measured service profiles determine the available budgets and the user-value conditions governing their welfare. 2.
